extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners interested in rural Black education, school founders, teachers, and philanthropic supporters
extracted.subtask_description: Memoir/history of founding and running Snow Hill Institute that contains practical principles and standards for community uplift, school governance, fundraising, and evaluation of teachers and graduates. Useful as guidance for building and sustaining rural, undenominational schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — general object
rubrics_metrics.description: This society shall be known as the Black Belt Improvement Society. Its object shall be the general uplift of the people of the Black Belt of Alabama; to make them better morally, mentally, spiritually, and financially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founding statement emphasizing broad, multidimensional uplift (moral, mental, spiritual, financial) as the Society's primary evaluative aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — eliminate credit system and encourage self-sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall further be the object of the Black Belt Improvement Society as far as possible, to eliminate the credit system from our social fabric; to stimulate in all members the desire to raise, as far as possible, all their food supplies at home, and pay cash for whatever may be purchased at the stores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes economic independence and cash-based purchasing; programmatic focus on home food production and avoidance of debt as measures of social/economic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — cooperative purchasing
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring about a system of co-operation in the purchase of what supplies cannot be raised at home wherever it can be done to advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages cooperative buying as a measurable practice to reduce costs and build community economic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — community discussion and education topics
rubrics_metrics.description: To discuss topics of interest to the communities in which the various societies may be organized, and topics relating to the general welfare of the race, and especially to farmers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monthly or regular meetings should cover locally relevant welfare and agricultural topics; effectiveness measured by community engagement and practical follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — strict economy and agricultural improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: To teach the people to practice the strictest economy, and especially to obtain and diffuse such information among farmers as shall lead to the improvement and diversification of crops, in order to create in farmers a desire for homes and better home conditions, and to stimulate a love for labor in both old and young. Each local organization may offer small prizes for the cleanest and best-kept house, the best pea-patch, and the best ear of corn, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes thrift, agricultural education, diversification, and incentives (small prizes) to change habits and create pride in homes and labor; concrete contests used as motivating metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — mutual aid fund for sickness and death
rubrics_metrics.description: To aid each other in sickness and in death; for this purpose a fee of ten cents will be collected from each member every month and held sacred to be used for no other purpose whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes a measurable mutual-aid mechanism (monthly fee) as a standard of community solidarity and practical welfare support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — stimulate home ownership and beautification
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall be one of the great objects of this society to stimulate its members to acquire homes, and urge those who already possess homes to improve and beautify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Home acquisition and improvement are explicit program goals; success can be tracked by new home purchases and home improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — purchase necessity-only policy
rubrics_metrics.description: To urge our members to purchase only the things that are absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioural standard promoting frugality and prioritization of needs over wants; used to measure personal and household economic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — moral/character reform
rubrics_metrics.description: To exert our every effort to obliterate those evils which tend to destroy our character and our homes, such as intemperance, gambling, and social impurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral reform is an explicit criterion of improvement; programs and meetings should address and reduce these vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Belt Improvement Society — civic responsibility and home standards
rubrics_metrics.description: To refrain from spending money and time foolishly or in unprofitable ways; to take an interest in the care of our highways, in the paying of our taxes and the education of our children; to plant shade trees, repair our yard fences, and in general, as far as possible, bring our home life up to the highest standard of civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide-ranging civic and home-care standards intended to raise living standards; actionable items (plant trees, repair fences, pay taxes) serve as concrete measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing committees and local meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: This Society has standing committees on Government, on Education, on Business, on Housekeeping, on Labor, and on Farming. The chairman of each of these committees holds monthly meetings in the various communities, at which time various topics pertaining to the welfare and uplift of the people are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational criterion: establish committees with regular (monthly) meetings focusing on specific domains; measure success by community adoption of discussed practices and inspiration produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: School denominational policy — undenominational stance
rubrics_metrics.description: I wanted that my school should be free from such 'isms.' I wanted a school for all the Negroes, thoroughly religious in its spirit, but entirely undenominational. For twenty-five years now we have adhered strictly to this policy. Many times when all was dark and there seemed to be no way, some of these denominations would come and offer me the money to run the work, provided I would accept their faith. But this I have never done, I had rather that the work should die than to sell my principle for money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: keep the school's religious spirit without denominational control; reject conditional donations that require students to adopt a particular faith. This is a normative standard for institutional independence and inclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership by example — model the behaviors you teach
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the cardinal points in Dr. Washington's Sunday evening talks to the students and teachers at Tuskegee was that they should buy homes of their own. I felt that the best way to teach the people to get a home was for me to own one myself. I thought that it would be useless for me to talk to them about buying homes as long as I did not have one for myself, so I secured a home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should model desired practices (e.g., home ownership) to credibly teach and encourage community adoption; 'do as I do' is treated as an effective pedagogical standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional worth measured by service (results over assets)
rubrics_metrics.description: But the worth of an institution is not judged by houses and land, but by its ability to serve the people among whom it is located. It has never been our end to acquire houses, land and industries, these we have used as means of enabling us to accomplish our end, which was and still is to seek and to save that which was lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary evaluation metric for the school is impact on people's lives (graduates' usefulness, improved homes, community influence), not physical property or wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated educational approach — religion, academics, and vocational training
rubrics_metrics.description: We have tolled our bells that they might hear, and preached the gospel of work in order that they might understand; we have used the church, the Sunday-School, Bible classes and other religious societies that they might feel; the class-rooms that they might know; the shops and farms that they might handle and do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum standard: combine spiritual instruction, academic teaching, and hands-on vocational/trade education (shops, farms) to achieve social service and practical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher evaluation — judge by results (Bagley's 'Testing Results')
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ultimate test of efficiency of efforts is the result of effort. ... That point is simply this: Does he 'make good' in results? Does he do the thing that he sets out to do, and does he do it well?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate teachers primarily by student outcomes and the tangible results of their teaching rather than by process-only measures or extraneous criteria (appearance, degrees, church membership). Use alumni success and practical competence as the salient measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundraising practices for small, undenominational schools
rubrics_metrics.description: In this house-to-house campaign for money, one must expect many rebuffs, but on the other hand one meets some of the finest people ... After winning the approval of the people in the community, both black and white, and getting whatever help I could from them, my thoughts turned towards the North for means to run the work. ... Dr. Washington wrote me to come to Tuskegee so as to accompany the Tuskegee Quartet North ... I was to tell what Tuskegee had done for me and was to show in turn what I was trying to do for my people. ... Through her appeals from time to time, we raised much money for our school. ... It was largely through Miss Messinger's appeals in the 'Transcript' that the people of Boston and New England learned of our work at the Snow Hill Institute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective fundraising combines local community approval, house-to-house canvassing, northern speaking tours, leveraging performing groups and prominent endorsers (e.g., Tuskegee Quartet, Dr. Washington), press coverage, personal storytelling, cultivating philanthropists (e.g., Messinger, Jeanes), and perseverance despite rebuffs. Do not accept donations that compromise core principles (e.g., conditional denominational support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alumni engagement and class giving as institutional measure
rubrics_metrics.description: So long before our time came, I wrote the members of my class telling them that it should be our aim to give Tuskegee $1000 at our Anniversary. They readily agreed with me and the class set itself to the task of raising the $1000. This was done ... I think in a small way it has served that purpose, because these class anniversary donations have never been less than $500 since that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set concrete fundraising goals for alumni classes as a metric of graduates' loyalty and institutional health; use anniversary gifts to encourage sustained giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key organizational roles and qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: In building up an institution such as we have done at Snow Hill, no one man is entitled to all the credit. ... Perhaps of these, the Trustees come first. ... Next to the Trustees, the officers and teachers have played a prominent part in the work here. My classmate, Henry A. Barnes, has been treasurer of the school for twenty-three years ... What Mr. Barnes has been to the Financial Department, Mr. R. A. Daly has been to our Industries. I consider Mr. Daly the best Industrial man that we can have. The Academic Department has been developed under the management of Messrs. Whitehead and Handy ... I cannot overestimate the value of the conscientious work done by my secretaries ... Much of the office work and responsibility fall upon the secretaries and this responsibility they have borne without complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for staffing and governance: active trustees, faithful treasurer, a strong industrial manager, capable academic leadership, and conscientious secretarial/office support are all essential indicators of institutional stability and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of press and peer networks to amplify support
rubrics_metrics.description: In speaking of our debt of gratitude to the forces that have helped in building up our work here, we must not overlook the press. There are certain great papers in this country that have been fearless in their advocacy of right and justice to the Negro, and have always opened their columns to any cause that has for its end the uplift of the lowly. Among these may be mentioned especially The New York Evening Post, The Boston Transcript, The Springfield Republican, The Hartford Courant, and in the South The Montgomery Advertiser. One also receives much aid and encouragement from those who are in similar work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate relationships with sympathetic newspapers and peer institutions; press advocacy and endorsements from other principals are measurable contributors to fundraising and public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduate outcomes as the metric of school success
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting those who have finished the course of study and others who have remained at the school long enough to catch its spirit and be influenced by its teaching, we have sent out into various parts of the South more than a thousand young men and women who are today leading useful and helpful lives. They are farmers, blacksmiths, wheelwrights, carpenters, housekeepers, dressmakers, printers, railway postal clerks, letter carriers, teachers, preachers, domestic servants, insurance agents, doctors, expressmen, contractors, timber-inspectors, college students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure institutional effectiveness by the variety and usefulness of graduates' occupations and civic contributions; the breadth of vocational outcomes is cited as direct evidence of success.
